title: AI Skill Threat: How the Structure of Developers' Beliefs about Software Development Ability Impacts Their Psychological Resilience During Rapid Technology Shift
title_aliases: The New Developer: AI Skill Threat, Identity Change & Developer Thriving in the Transition to AI-Assisted Software Development
date_basis: Supplied PDF draft date and OSF version-2 submission date, both 15 March 2025; source page inspected in local Chrome on 13 October 2026. Last-edited date (27 August 2025) is separate.
verification_scope: User-supplied 55-page PDF: title, abstract, recruitment, measures, principal results and limitations; OSF page and embedded first PDF page inspected in local Chrome to match the artifact and version. Data and preregistered analysis were not independently reanalyzed.
summary: An observational survey of 3,267 developers and technical managers relates competitive and innate-brilliance beliefs to reported AI-related identity threat, and learning culture and belonging to more favorable reported experiences. It also identifies differences in concerns and intended upskilling across groups.
limitations: Volunteer recruitment including Pluralsight users, self-report outcomes, optional demographic responses and cross-sectional mediation limit causal interpretation. The study does not measure delivered software, demonstrate permanent skill loss, prove that a culture intervention works, or establish that AI skepticism is irrational. Authors' Developer Success Lab/Pluralsight affiliations are relevant context.
version_note: OSF version 2 displays the older The New Developer title but embeds the supplied revised-title PDF. Preserve both titles; do not count versions as separate studies. The version DOI resolves to OSF and Crossref confirms the older registered title and 2025 year. An initial DataCite lookup returned 404 because that registry does not hold this DOI; it is not evidence of an unregistered DOI.

title: Self-Regulated AI Use Hinders Long-Term Learning
date_basis: Local Chrome SSRN page: posted 16 October 2025, written 1 October 2025, revised 1 August 2026. Citation year describes first posting; results describe the supplied 2026 revision.
verification_scope: User-supplied 63-page PDF: title, abstract, experimental design, main results and Table 1, mediation assumptions, boundary conditions and selected appendix details on Stockfish and attrition; SSRN dates, bylines and identifier matched in local Chrome. No data reanalysis.
summary: A preregistered chess-training experiment compares automatic AI tips with the same tips plus optional answer-revealing help. Among 216 completers from 306 recruits, the optional-help group had smaller unaided test-score gains after 12 weeks of training. Both randomized groups received AI; the comparison isolates assistance design, not AI versus no AI.
limitations: Stockfish-based chess assistance, not a general-purpose LLM or programming intervention. Main analysis is of completers, with approximately 29% attrition; reported absence of differential attrition does not remove every selection concern. The 30% versus 64% figures are relative changes in bounded test-game scores, not percentages of underlying skill. Causal mediation needs additional assumptions; the nonparticipant comparison is observational.
version_note: Supplied PDF matches the 63-page SSRN revision dated 1 August 2026. The 2026 Academy of Management proceedings abstract is related coverage, not independent evidence or proof that this full manuscript is a peer-reviewed journal article.

document_verification.scope: Methods, principal results, limitations and selected appendices; no independent replication

title: Does Working with AI Agents Change How Developers Code, Test, and Review?
container_title: 20th International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2026)
date_basis: Primary Dagstuhl publication metadata dated 5 October 2026, checked 13 October 2026.
verification_scope: Publisher metadata and linked 13-page published PDF: abstract, methods, results/Tables 1-5 and discussion; compared with user-supplied 12-page SSRN preprint. Replication package not executed.
summary: AIDev-based comparisons of 669 developer-repository pairs in agent-exposed repositories with 228 control pairs find increased PR-description length and small test-change associations. Apparent review changes in before/after comparisons do not remain significant after comparison with controls. This challenges simple attribution of every review trend to agents, without establishing better delivered software.
limitations: Nonrandom adoption defined by first visible agent PR, not first AI use; selection of persistent contributors and active reviewers, median-split controls and limited matching weaken causal identification. Description length and test-file heuristics do not measure explanation quality or defect prevention. Null review contrasts do not establish equivalence. Reporting questions in the time-window and misattribution summaries are logged for clarification; no replication was run.
version_note: Published in the Emerging Results, Vision & Reflection Track on 5 October 2026. SSRN 6996078 and 7070979 are earlier versions of this study, not additional evidence. Shares the AIDev dataset family with other repository studies, but its analytic samples and outcomes differ.

document_verification.scope: Publisher metadata, abstract, methods, results and discussion; compared with supplied preprint
